data.text/markdown: ← 4. Contracts

5. Pipelines and engines

Say the Monday report the sales team presents reads orders by city, which read the cleaned orders, which read the raw orders feed. A few hundred orders change every hour, and a bad row anywhere below ends up on their slides. Recomputing every layer each time is slow, and hand-written incremental logic ("process the rows where updated_at is newer than…") misses deletes and late rows until the analyst finds totals that no longer add up. Next quarter the platform team also wants the job on another engine. We'll keep a join up to date from its changes alone, stack transforms into layers that pass only their changes along, run the same checked plans on several engines, and look at how the model treats doubles, time and text.

Keeping a join up to date

Incremental view maintenance computes the change to a result from the changes to its inputs. A source piped into a transform is a node, and node.refresh() keeps it up to date with update rules proved in Lean. We write the query once, as an Ibis transform, pipe one source into it and pass the other by keyword. The sources are in-memory tables (StaticSource, from sverify.io); Delta and Iceberg tables work the same way (chapter 1 reads a Delta table).

data.text/markdown:
What is maintained, and what is recomputed

Filters, computed columns, inner joins (self-joins too), cross joins, UNION ALL and ORDER BY are maintained from their changes. Left, semi and anti joins (a left join's NULL-padded rows must be retracted when a match turns up later), DISTINCT, LIMIT (it depends on row order), windows and aggregates are recomputed and diffed on every refresh. Contracts work on all of them, and the result is correct; the cost is a full run per refresh. node.status() says which kind of node you have:

data.text/markdown:
A recomputed node's change, the difference between its new and its old result, still flows to the nodes that read it. The view is a table like any other: view.table is an Ibis table to query further, and to_arrow(), to_polars() and to_pandas() return its rows. Nodes are built from Ibis transforms; a view written as a SQL string has no public counterpart yet.

Delta rules in brief

Every row carries a weight: +1 for an inserted row, -1 for a deleted one, and an update is a delete plus an insert. A table with weights is a Z-set, and adding a batch of changes means summing the weights per row. Filter and project treat each row on its own, so their change is the same query run on the changes only (theorem Rel.zeval_add). A join pairs rows from two tables. If both change, the new result has four kinds of pairs:
old customers B new customers ΔB
old orders A A × B: in the old result A × ΔB: new
new orders ΔA ΔA × B: new ΔA × ΔB: new
The change to the join is ΔA × B + ΔA × ΔB + A × ΔB. Hand-written pipelines often forget the corner term. We'll apply the changes "delete order 1, update order 2 from 5 to 20, insert order 4" to the orders, and "insert cy, delete bob" to the customers, with the corner term on and off:

data.text/markdown: With the switch off, the pair "order 4 and customer cy" is missing, since both are new and only the corner term produces it. Phantom bob rows appear too, one with weight -1: the updated order 2 was paired with the old bob, and only the corner term cancels that pairing with bob's deletion. Lean proves the full rule once. Rel.delta generates the update plan as an ordinary plan that reads the old tables and the change tables, and Rel.delta_correct proves it computes exactly the change. Any engine can run it. sverify.engines.delta_plans(view.internal_plan) returns the plans of our view. orders$delta and customers$delta are the change tables, with a trailing __weight column; old tables get weight 1 (Project +[1]), and the join multiplies weights ($3 * $6):

data.text/markdown: On each refresh, substrait-check --delta builds the update plan (Rel.delta), splits it into pieces without UNION ALL (Rel.terms) and encodes each row's weight as the __weight column (Rel.weighted, with Rel.weighted_eval covering an ordinary engine). Sverify registers the change tables, runs the plans, sums the weights per row and merges the result into the view. A batch is computed completely before anything is replaced, so a failure changes nothing. A change that can't happen, such as deleting a row that doesn't exist, is refused by the source, and neither the source nor the view moves:

The theorems cover the Lean model. Randomized tests cover the rest (the JSON translation, the Python glue, the engine): they generate random tables and batches with NULLs and duplicates, and after every batch compare the maintained view with a recompute, as the button does. view.refresh(audit=True) runs the same comparison in production and raises AuditError (from sverify.errors) before applying a wrong batch.

Pipelines

Real pipelines are layered: cleaned tables feed joined tables feed reports. In sverify the layers are transforms piped from the one below, so the code reads in the order the data flows: orders.pipe(paid).pipe(doubled) is the same node as doubled(paid(orders)), and the other inputs of a layer come by keyword. Without a .write in between, transforms fuse into one plan, maintained as one incremental view. .write(sink) stores a layer, and the layers above read the stored table as a versioned source through its change feed. An intermediate result is computed once and shared, and only changes flow through the layers. The base layer carries the contracts of chapter 4, and their guarantees hold in every state.

data.text/markdown:
When the data breaks the contract

A refused batch stops the report until someone fixes the feed. For a few bad rows among thousands, you may rather set them aside and let the rest through. With on_violation="quarantine" on the transform (or on the source), the refresh sets aside the rows that break a precondition, with the reason, and the node runs on the others (#184). A row is set aside when a row condition is not TRUE on it, or when another row shares its key: both rows of a repeated id go, so the rule needs no order between them. Every precondition holds on the rows that stay (Catalog.kept_sound in Quarantine.lean), so paid's proof holds as before. We feed a Delta table an order with a negative amount and one with an id that exists already:

console.text:

  requires orders: (_.amount >= 0) (checked on data)
  requires orders: unique(id) (checked on data)
  view clean: orders@v1
  quarantine: orders: 3 row(s) quarantined (2 × unique(id), 1 × (_.amount >= 0)), 3 in quarantine at /tmp/tmptix37x8q/clean_quarantine

data.text/markdown:
The refresh completed (outcome is 'quarantined'). Order 4 went through. Order 5 breaks amount >= 0. Order 2 is now on two rows, so both copies are set aside, the one clean held before included, until the feed says which is right. The rows sit in a Delta table next to the sink, clean_quarantine, with the reason and the source version, and clean_orders.quarantined() returns them. A scheduled job posts flagged.alert() to whoever is on call, for example as a GitHub issue:

data.text/markdown: on_violation="hold" holds the node at its versions instead: the refresh commits nothing for the batch, says why (outcome is "held"), and reads the batch again next time. The default, "error", is what the buttons above do. A change to the schema breaks a contract in another way. Say the feed's owner lets id be NULL, and the next version has an order without one. clean was proved with id NOT NULL, so the refresh refuses, and the message names the column, the version and the contract:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
SchemaError: `orders.id` became nullable at v1, and the new rows have NULLs in it; `keyed` was proved with it NOT NULL. Fix the upstream, or handle NULLs in `keyed` (e.g. `.fill_null(0)`) and relax `requires`.
The schema of orders changed incompatibly; views ['keyed'] have contracts proved against the old schema: build the pipeline again.

data.text/markdown:
Why the guarantees survive every batch

Whoever reads base relies on its guarantees on the hundredth batch as on the first. paid's preconditions were checked on all of orders once, on the first refresh. After that only the batch is checked: row conditions (amount >= 0) on the inserted rows, and keys (unique(id)) among the inserted rows and against the keys of the rows the batch keeps. Theorem Spec.update in Compose.lean says a table's contract survives a batch under exactly these checks, and Triple.maintained says a contracted view's guarantees then hold in the new state. So base satisfies doubled ≥ 0 and is non-NULL after every batch without re-checking the whole table, and the Delta table it is written to records those guarantees with every version, for the layers that read it. The layering is Rel.chain_sound (DBSP's chain rule): when a view reads another view's stored result and gets that view's change as its change table, its own update plan is still correct. For a recomputed view, ZSet.diff_correct shows that new − old is a valid change to pass on. Each refresh brings the layers up to date upstream first and writes every stored node once per state. After a restart, building the same nodes and refreshing resumes each stored node from its table when the plan and the source versions match.

Your own source and sink

Say the customers don't live in the lake. The CRM team has an API that returns the customers who signed up after a given time, and finance wants the city report as a Parquet file on their share. A source you write is one method, read(since), which returns the new rows and a cursor for the next read. A sink is one method, write(change), which stores what a refresh hands it. Sverify numbers the reads as versions, works out what changed, checks the preconditions and decides when a state needs writing. We read the CRM with from_query, which keeps a high-water mark on a column, and write the report with a sink that keeps the contract next to the file, so a restarted job knows what it already wrote:

  wrote city_report from base@v2, crm@v1: overwrite, 2 row(s) written, 0 deleted

data.text/markdown: The first refresh read the CRM in full as version 1 and wrote the file. The second read only bob, as version 2, and the report says what that rests on: customers only arrive with a greater signed_up. That is the watermark job's assumption from chapter 1, and it can break. A sign-up the CRM records late, with an earlier time, falls below the cursor and is never read. We record one and audit, which reads the source again in full up to the cursor and compares it with what the batches built:

  base@v2: no new version

AuditError: crm@v2 differs from the table read again in full: its batches missed rows; nothing was applied

data.text/markdown:
The plain refresh saw nothing new, and the audit caught the row the cursor skipped and applied nothing. A source can promise no more than its reads do, so give it an assumes= that says what its batches rely on, and audit now and then. The rest of the toolkit, in sverify.io:
  • from_frame(fn) reads the whole table on every refresh and diffs it against the last read, so the change is exact and nothing is assumed. from_files(path) reads the files that are new in a directory. Subclass Source for anything else. A batch can be a whole table (kind="snapshot") or rows added and removed (kind="changes").
  • A sink's write gets a SinkChange: the rows added and removed since its last write, or the whole table on the first, with the contract to record. contract() reads that contract back, so each state is written once even across restarts; without it sverify remembers for the life of the process. sink_from(fn) hands the whole table to a function.
  • These sources have no metadata, so preconditions on them are checked on the rows, and they keep the table in memory. A restarted job reads them in full again and numbers its versions above the ones its sinks recorded. A table format with statistics and a change feed implements the full VersionedSource protocol, as Delta and Iceberg do.
  • Storage holds object store options, or a function that fetches fresh ones, shared by every table that needs them.

Engines and SQL

A proof is about the Lean model. Whether an engine computes what the model says is a separate question, and engines disagree about NULL join keys, NaN, integer overflow, the rounding of integer division and the order of ties. Plans come from one producer: the vendored Ibis producer, or sverify's lift of DuckDB's SQL (SQLGlot) for SQL strings. They run on these engines:
engine how the plan runs status
"duckdb" (default) the SQL generator (sverify.engines.to_sql) writes the plan as DuckDB SQL Tier 1: characterized against the model, translation proved
"polars" a translator turns the plan into a Polars LazyFrame, run on Polars's streaming engine Tier 2: characterized, shims proved
"datafusion" DataFusion's Substrait consumer (the sverify[datafusion] extra) Tier 2
"spark", or a Spark session the SQL generator writes Spark SQL (the sverify[spark] extra) Tier 2
Snowflake SQL only, checked on the fakesnow emulator Tier 3
The tiers are explained in the README. Work on DataFusion, Spark and Snowflake is paused until the generated lowerings land (#241, then #271), and the tests use DuckDB as their oracle. DuckDB and Polars are characterized fact by fact, each fact with its evidence (the ledgers). DuckDB and Polars run Lean's written form of the plan (sverify.engines.written_plan), so what runs is what was checked, and their translators spell out the model's semantics instead of taking engine defaults. We'll line the engines up. Pick a query, and each engine runs the same checked plan (sverify.engines.run(con, plan, engine)) next to Lean's reference interpreter:

data.text/markdown:
What to look for:
  • NULL join keys never match, because NULL = NULL is not TRUE. Each translator says so explicitly.
  • Integer division truncates toward zero, as in DuckDB's // and in Lean (-7 // 2 = -3). Polars' own // floors to -4, so its translator truncates.
  • NaN is one value, equal to itself and above every number, so NaN > 0 is TRUE. The next section covers doubles.
  • qty + 1 on the largest integer is where engines differ most: DataFusion wraps around to the smallest integer, while the Polars and DuckDB translators raise, as the reference does. An integer that leaves its declared width is an error, and verify reports it beforehand.
Lean's column is missing for the last two queries. The model stores a double as a very large integer code (SubstraitLean/Float.lean), so the checker's printer can't tell a double from an integer beyond 64 bits. The test suite compares doubles through the engines.

Choosing the engine for a node

A node doesn't fix its engine. The plan is the same everywhere, and node.refresh(engine="polars") (or "datafusion", "spark", a Spark session) picks where it runs; DuckDB in memory is the default. A node keeps its state between refreshes, so the next refresh may use another engine. Contracts checked on data take engine= too: @sv.transform(ensures=[...], on_unproved="check", check_engine="duckdb"). We refresh a fresh node of the NULL-key join on each engine:

Every engine returns the same rows, and the NULL key matches nothing.

Routes: how a proof reaches an engine

A proof is about the plan under one semantics, the reference by default. report.run(con, engine, route="auto") and node.refresh(engine=..., route="auto") choose how it reaches the engine, and refuse the plan with the reason where nothing does (D13 in core-semantics.md). The route names the plan's class on the engine: exact (every result the engine gives, the reference allows), observed (equal under an observation the postcondition states, a float tolerance included), shim (after a proved translation) or refused. Before the plan runs, its preconditions are checked on the data. We take the join to Polars:
Route on Polars: exact; evidence tested

A stored node also needs a rerun to reproduce its result, since its sink commits each epoch once. The sink states what that means: exact bits (reproducible=sv.equivalent()), or doubles within a tolerance, DeltaSink(uri, reproducible=sv.equivalent(floats=sv.within(abs=1e-6))), for a SUM of doubles, which Polars's streaming engine may add in another order each run. A refresh whose route cannot meet that is refused. The examples show both, step by step.

SQL for DuckDB, Snowflake and Spark

When the data lives in a warehouse, the plan goes to the warehouse. sverify.engines.to_sql writes a checked plan, or one of Lean's update plans, as SQL whose result is Rel.eval of the plan. Columns are positional (c0, c1, …), filters keep only TRUE rows (IS TRUE), integers are checked at their declared width and every ORDER BY says where NULLs go. Each engine's differences go through a Dialect:

SELECT
  s1."c0" AS "k",
  s1."c1" AS "doubled"
FROM (
  SELECT
    s2."c3" AS "c0",
    s2."c4" AS "c1"
  FROM (
    SELECT
      s3."c0" AS "c0",
      s3."c1" AS "c1",
      s3."c2" AS "c2",
      s3."c0" AS "c3",
      (
        CAST(s3."c1" AS BIGINT) * CAST(2 AS BIGINT)
      ) AS "c4"
    FROM (
      SELECT
        s4."c0" AS "c0",
        s4."c1" AS "c1",
        s4."c2" AS "c2"
      FROM (
        SELECT
          "k" AS "c0",
          "qty" AS "c1",
          (
            "v" + CAST('0' AS DOUBLE)
          ) AS "c2"
        FROM "t"
      ) AS s4
      WHERE
        (
          (
            CAST(0 AS BIGINT) < s4."c1"
          ) IS TRUE
        )
    ) AS s3
  ) AS s2
) AS s1

Try select k, row_number() over (partition by k order by qty) as rn from t in each dialect. DuckDB gets an ordinal column, so ties break the way Lean's stable sort breaks them. Snowflake and Spark refuse, because their tables have no row order. When a contract report says deterministic (chapter 4), deterministic=True promises there are no ties and the SQL is written. Snowflake: integers are NUMBER(38,0) checked against the 64-bit range, timestamps are TIMESTAMP_NTZ(6), every identifier is quoted, and interval-valued result columns are refused because Snowflake has no interval type. Spark and Databricks: the dialect (sverify.engines.SPARK) targets Spark 4 and is also what node.refresh(engine="spark") runs. It assumes the session settings of sverify.engines.SPARK_CONF, above all spark.sql.ansi.enabled: without ANSI mode an overflow wraps around and a bad cast gives NULL. Spark answers several questions its own way, and the SQL spells out or refuses each:
  • / of integers is a double, so division is div. / of doubles raises on a zero divisor, as the reference does; a plan that asks for IEEE gets ±inf or NaN from a CASE.
  • CAST(9.3e18 AS BIGINT) saturates, and FLOOR and CEIL return integers. Each is range-checked or repaired.
  • SUM of BIGINT raises on an overflowing partial sum even when the total fits, so it adds DECIMAL(38,0).
  • TIMESTAMP is the session time zone's, and so is what date_trunc returns, so the SQL stays in TIMESTAMP_NTZ.
  • POWER of doubles is Java's Math.pow (within 1 ulp of C's) and is refused, as are sorts and windows over a table without deterministic=True.
Spark runs locally, unlike Snowflake. The tests run every coverage case and every query of the Snowflake suite on a local Spark session (Java 17 or 21) and compare them with Rel.eval. The Lean evaluator is the specification: the suite runs every fixture and every update plan on DataFusion, Polars and DuckDB with random tables, and compares them with each other and with Rel.eval, row for row in Lean's order where order matters. The Snowflake SQL is parsed and run on fakesnow. The engine profiles list where each engine departs from the model.

Doubles, time and text

Say one of your sensors sends NaN, or a timestamp lands at the edge of the calendar. Floating-point measurements, timestamps and strings each have traps, and the Lean model pins them down bit for bit where it matters, because a proof about the wrong semantics proves nothing.

Doubles: NaN, infinities and one zero

In IEEE 754 comparisons and in Python, NaN equals nothing, itself included. SQL engines (PostgreSQL, DuckDB, Spark, Snowflake) order doubles differently, and so does the model:
−∞ < … < 0.0 < … < +∞ < NaN
There is one NaN, equal to itself and larger than every number, and one zero: −0.0 is 0.0, so -0.0 >= 0 holds and −0.0 never shows in a result. DataFusion's own order, f64::total_cmp, splits both, so sverify stores DataFusion's tables the model's way (docs/how-it-works.md). Here is a table with both zeros and NaN:

data.text/markdown: Two consequences. v > 0 keeps NaN rows, so a filter meant as "positive readings" lets glitches through, and only an upper bound (v < 1e9, say) removes NaN. And the table was given both zeros and holds one: DISTINCT keeps a single zero and -1 * 0.0 is 0.0, on every engine. Lean models doubles exactly, as integer codes in the same order, so the proofs know all of this. We build a filter and see whether "no NaN" follows:

data.text/html:
NOT proved: 1 of 3 postconditions not proved
semantics: reference
postcondition status
~_.v.isnan() ❌ it may be FALSE on some rows; fails on m(v) = [(nan,)] gives (v) = [(nan,)]
(_.v != -9999.0) ✅ proved
_.v.notnull() ✅ proved
output column known values
v a double > 0.0
kept rows

data.text/markdown: Comparisons with constants are exact, sentinels like -9999.0 and the boundary between v > 0.5 and v >= 0.5 included. Arithmetic on doubles (v * 2.5) is known only to give some double, because rounding isn't modelled. The reference raises where an operation on finite doubles overflows to ±∞, so the report assumes v * 2.5 stays finite and the run checks it on the data first: a ±∞ in a result came from the data (#575). For the same reason power(-inf, 0.5) and a MEDIAN between −∞ and +∞ raise, where engines disagree. FLOOR, CEIL, ROUND and the cast to an integer are exact and monotone, so a bounded double rounds to a bounded integer:

data.text/html:
proved
semantics: reference
postcondition status
~_.v.isnan() ✅ proved
(_.scaled >= 0) ✅ proved
(_.rounded >= 0) ✅ proved
(_.rounded <= 1) ✅ proved
output column known values
v a double ≥ 0.0 and ≤ 1.0
scaled a double ≥ 0.0 and < 2.500000000000002

data.text/markdown:
Timestamps and intervals

Timestamps are microseconds since 1970 (UTC) in the model, and intervals are durations. Comparisons with literals, ts + interval, ts1 - ts0 and joins on time are tracked like integers. The calendar functions are computed exactly on the Gregorian calendar (Time.lean), and Lean proves they grow with the timestamp, so a range of timestamps gives a range of years and of truncated months. Pick a time window and see what Lean derives:

data.text/html:
columnwhat Lean knows
tsa timestamp in [2024-03-01 00:00:00, 2024-03-31 23:59:59.999999]
yearthe integer 2024
houran integer in [0, 23]
month_starta timestamp = 2024-03-01 00:00:00
week_starta timestamp in [2024-02-26 00:00:00, 2024-03-25 00:00:00]
a_minute_latera timestamp in [2024-03-01 00:01:00, 2024-04-01 00:00:59.999999]

data.text/markdown: Within one calendar year, year is that exact integer. Truncations stay inside the window's range, rounded down, and hour is in [0, 23], a proved range that doesn't grow with the timestamp. Without the filter, truncating to a month may fail near the ends of the timestamp range, so the plan needs ts between 1678 and 2262, the range of nanosecond timestamps. Sverify works it out and asks you to declare it (chapter 4 shows how inferred bounds work):

data.text/html:
NOT proved: 2 preconditions needed
semantics: reference
postcondition status
needs ❌ (.ts >= datetime(1678, 1, 1)) and (.ts < datetime(2262, 1, 1)) on events, inferred from ts.truncate('month') (overflow otherwise): declare them in requires (each run then checks them on the data), or rewrite so no row needs them (events.filter((_.ts >= datetime(1678, 1, 1)) & (_.ts < datetime(2262, 1, 1))) first, or a CASE); on_inferred='warn' assumes them instead
output column known values
month_start a timestamp in [1678-01-01 00:00:00, 2261-12-01 00:00:00] or NULL

Text

Strings are sequences of Unicode characters in the model. substring, strpos, character_length, trim, || and LIKE are computed exactly, and the test suite checks them against DuckDB on random strings. Here is Lean's Rel.eval next to DuckDB, running Ibis's own SQL, on some awkward words:

data.text/markdown: UPPER, LOWER and regular expressions are black boxes: Lean knows they return a string (or a boolean), and no proof depends on which one, because Unicode case mapping and regex engines are large and engine-specific. A regular expression is a possible runtime error unless Lean can see that it compiles. Patterns in a conservative subset of Rust's syntax are accepted, and anything fancier is reported. A back-reference like \1 isn't supported by DataFusion's engine at all:

data.text/html:
NOT proved: 1 possible runtime error
semantics: reference
postcondition status
(_.n >= 0) ✅ proved
_.shout.notnull() ✅ proved
runtime ❌ may fail: invalid regular expression: REGEXP_MATCH_"(a|b)\1"(word)
hint sverify found no bound on an input column that rules it out: the inference does not cover this kind of invalid regular expression
output column known values
n an integer in [0, 4294967296]
shout a string
has_digits TRUE or FALSE
repeated TRUE or FALSE

data.text/markdown: Contracts don't track string contents yet: startswith('acc') in a filter doesn't let Lean prove startswith('ac') afterwards. Lengths, NULLs and errors are tracked. You can now keep a join up to date from its changes, stack contracted transforms into layers that pass only their changes along, and rely on their guarantees in every state while only each batch is checked. You can refresh a node on DuckDB, Polars, DataFusion or Spark, hand a plan to Snowflake as SQL, and tell where an engine could depart from the model. That is the end of the tour. The guide covers every feature in more detail, and how it works goes under the hood: the checker, the producers and engines, and what is proved and what is trusted.
